title: James Bond Producer Barbara Broccoli to Be President of U.K.’s National Film and Television School
description: James Bond producer Barbara Broccoli has been revealed as the next president of the U.K.’s National Film and Television School. She succeeds Oscar-
body:
James Bond producer Barbara Broccoli has been revealed as the next president of the U.K.’s National Film and Television School. She succeeds Oscar-winning producer David Puttnam in the role.

	Broccoli will be the first female president in the NFTS’s history. Puttnam, whose credits include “Chariots of Fire,” “The Killing Fields” and “Midnight Express,” is to take on an honorary role as president emeritus.


	News of her appointment comes ahead of the opening of the Cubby Broccoli Building at the school’s Beaconsfield campus in January 2027. It is named after her father, legendary producer Albert R. “Cubby” Broccoli, who established the James Bond franchise. The building will provide state-of-the-art teaching facilities, specialist creative spaces and the school’s first purpose-built, fully accessible on-site student accommodation.
	

	Broccoli said, “It’s a tremendous honor to become president of the National Film and Television School, following in Lord David Puttnam’s footsteps. Having been involved with the NFTS for many years, I have seen first-hand the extraordinary talent it develops and the vital role it plays in shaping the future of our industry. With the opening of the Cubby Broccoli Building taking place in January, this is especially meaningful. My father believed in the power of filmmaking and in giving talented people the opportunity to succeed.”

	Puttnam said, “I could not be happier than to be handing over the presidency of the NFTS to my close friend Barbara. To leave the school in such good hands is repaying the last of the many debts I owe to my predecessor Richard Attenborough. My long relationship with the school, and the challenges we’ve faced and overcome has in many ways defined my career. I’d like to pay a special tribute to those many, many colleagues who have helped make the NFTS the most rewarding journey of my life.”

schema.headline: James Bond Producer Barbara Broccoli to Be President of U.K.’s National Film and Television School

title: Palme d’Or Winner ‘Fjord’ to Open 26th European Film Festival Malaysia, Astro First to Stream Selected Titles
description:
Cristian Mungiu’s Palme d’Or winner “Fjord” will open the 26th European Film Festival Malaysia (EUFF) on Nov. 26 at TGV Pavilion Kuala Lumpur. 

	T
body:
Cristian Mungiu’s Palme d’Or winner “Fjord” will open the 26th European Film Festival Malaysia (EUFF) on Nov. 26 at TGV Pavilion Kuala Lumpur. 

	This year, for the first time, some of the festival’s films will also go to home audiences through Malaysian media and entertainment group Astro.

	The festival runs through Dec. 13 under the theme “Atlas.” Its 20 films represent 20 countries. Eight of them premiered at Cannes, and three come from last year’s Venice competition.
	

	Astro, one of this year’s official partners, will release a selection of the 20 titles on Astro First, its premium home cinema service, from January 2027. The titles going to the service have not been named yet.

	“Audiences today are more discerning, with interests that go beyond familiar genres, languages and cultures,” said Henry Tan, group CEO of Astro. He added that the Astro First release would “bring these films beyond the cinema and into homes across Malaysia, reaching audiences who may not otherwise have the opportunity to experience them.”

	In “Fjord,” Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve lead the cast as members of a devout Romanian family. After the family moves to Norway, the way they bring up their children comes under scrutiny. It is Mungiu’s second Palme d’Or. Reinsve can also be seen in Joachim Trier’s “Sentimental Value,” which took the Grand Prix at Cannes in 2025 and won the Academy Award for best international feature this year.

	Two more films come from this year’s Cannes competition. Asghar Farhadi’s “Parallel Tales” stars Isabelle Huppert and Catherine Deneuve, and Rodrigo Sorogoyen’s “The Beloved” stars Javier Bardem. Sandra Wollner’s “Everytime,” which won in Un Certain Regard, is also on the program.
	

	The Venice titles include Paolo Sorrentino’s “La Grazia,” which won Toni Servillo the Volpi Cup, and Ildikó Enyedi’s “Silent Friend.” That film stars Tony Leung Chiu-wai and Léa Seydoux and won the Fipresci Prize. Rounding out the selection are the Dardenne brothers’ “Young Mothers” and László Nemes’ “Orphan.” Pierre Monnard’s “Hello Betty,” a Swiss biopic, will close the festival.

	“Many of these films arrive with cinema’s highest honors, but what moved us most was how, placed side by side, they began to speak to one another,” said Yu Ern Chia, EUFF’s festival director. “Almost without planning it, this year’s selection returned again and again to family. These are European stories, but Malaysian audiences will find their own questions in them.”

	The Delegation of the European Union to Malaysia runs the festival with Blackflag, which created and produces the “Polis Evo” films, one of Malaysia’s highest-grossing franchises. The 2026 edition opens a four-year partnership between the two that runs through 2029. Seventeen EU member states are taking part, together with Norway, Switzerland and Ukraine. The National Film Development Corporation Malaysia (FINAS), TGV Cinemas and Astro are official partners.

	“Our collaboration embodies the European Union’s motto, ‘United in diversity,’ celebrating the richness of Europe’s different cultures and creative voices, while bringing them together through the universal language of cinema,” said Rafael Daerr, the EU’s ambassador to Malaysia.

	EUFF started around the turn of the millennium. In its early years, the embassies of EU member states in Malaysia organized it. Since then it has screened hundreds of European films, held editions in Penang, Kuching and Kota Kinabalu as well as Kuala Lumpur, and gone online during the pandemic. Organizers say it may be the oldest foreign film festival in Malaysia that is still running.

	Blackflag has also been releasing world cinema in Malaysia. It recently partnered with GSC International Screens on a release of Edward Yang’s “Yi Yi: A One and a Two,” and with Guangzhou Film Expo and Guangzhou Performance / Film Ltd. on Chinese Film Week 2025.

schema.headline: Palme d’Or Winner ‘Fjord’ to Open 26th European Film Festival Malaysia, Astro First to Stream Selected Titles

title: Nicole Kidman to Receive Honorary Cesar From French Film Academy
description: Nicole Kidman will receive an honorary Cesar at France’s Cesar Awards, with the presentation set for the 52nd ceremony on Feb. 25, 2027, at the Oly
body:
Nicole Kidman will receive an honorary Cesar at France’s Cesar Awards, with the presentation set for the 52nd ceremony on Feb. 25, 2027, at the Olympia in Paris.

	The Académie des Arts et Techniques du Cinéma, the French film academy behind the awards, announced the honor on Thursday alongside broadcaster Canal+. The two said the award recognizes an actor and producer who has never allowed fame to steer the work she chooses.


	Kidman is both a Hollywood star and a major name in auteur cinema. The filmmakers she has worked with range from Stanley Kubrick and Jane Campion to Lars von Trier, Baz Luhrmann and Yorgos Lanthimos.
	

	The Australian actor first broke through internationally with “Dead Calm” and went on to star in “Moulin Rouge!,” “Eyes Wide Shut,” “The Others” and “Dogville.” She won the best actress Oscar in 2003 for playing Virginia Woolf in “The Hours.” In 2024, she took the Volpi Cup for best actress at the Venice Film Festival for “Babygirl.”

	Kidman also produces. She co-founded Blossom Films, the company behind series including “Big Little Lies,” “The Undoing” and “Nine Perfect Strangers,” all of which she also headlined. 

	On stage, she won critical praise in London’s West End for “The Blue Room” and “Photograph 51.”

	Her previous honors include being named a Companion of the Order of Australia in 2006 and receiving the Cannes Film Festival’s 70th anniversary prize in 2017. In 2024, the American Film Institute gave her its Life Achievement Award, making her the first Australian to receive it.

	Away from the screen, Kidman serves as a UN Women goodwill ambassador. She has also helped raise several million dollars for women’s cancer programs, including at Stanford and the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center.
	

	Canal+ will carry the Feb. 25 tribute live and exclusively, unencrypted for all viewers.

schema.headline: Nicole Kidman to Receive Honorary Cesar From French Film Academy

title: Lei Lei’s Hybrid Doc ‘Vertigo Garden,’ About a Botanist’s AI-Replicated Memories, Lands at Asian Shadows Ahead of IDFA Bow (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Boutique sales company Asian Shadows has acquired “Vertigo Garden,” the new feature from Chinese filmmaker and animation artist Lei Lei, ahead of i
body:
Boutique sales company Asian Shadows has acquired “Vertigo Garden,” the new feature from Chinese filmmaker and animation artist Lei Lei, ahead of its world premiere in the Envision Competition at the International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam (IDFA).

	This is Lei’s second feature. IDFA has also nominated it for the Beeld en Geluid IDFA ReFrame Award, which honors creative work with archival material.


	“Vertigo Garden” unfolds at the Lushan Botanical Garden and follows the life of its botanist. His body is found in the snow and ice at the top of Lushan Mountain, with both body and brain intact. Scientists study the brain, use AI to reproduce his memories and set them loose in a digital world. Through conversation, the film pieces together the botanist’s storied bond with the metasequoia tree and his efforts to communicate with the planet’s memories through these ancient trees.
	

	Lei uses the metasequoia to probe how memory, life and the planet connect, combining documentary, 3D animation and experimental techniques.

	“I believe that Asian Shadows and its team truly love the film. They will treat this film like their own child and promote it to meet audiences around the world, which for me goes beyond what is called a business partnership,” Lei said.

	In a director’s statement, Lei wrote that he started filming at the garden, in his hometown, with an 8mm camera in 2024, making long-term field recordings there. He credited Chris Marker’s “Sans Soleil” (1983) as the inspiration for the screenplay, and the film uses video letters to stage an imagined correspondence between the filmmaker and the botanist. The statement also set out plans to 3D-scan metasequoia fossils, trunks and the garden’s greenhouse, then move through the digital models with a virtual camera to create effects that resemble a video game. Elsewhere, Lei described training AI to generate footage of the same location again and again, cutting the results into a flickering effect he likened to the work of artist Rose Lowder.
	

	Lei wrote and produced the film with Chai Mi. It is produced by See-Ray Studio Production, the animation and visual art company Lei founded.

	Maria A. Ruggieri, head of sales and acquisitions at Asian Shadows, called Lei a singular voice among Chinese filmmakers without any doubt. “His talent as an animator, his search for new representations of China, his love and care for the recreation of lost emotions and history are perfectly assembled one more time in ‘Vertigo Garden,'” she said.

	Born in Nanchang, Lei earned a master’s degree in animation from Tsinghua University. He went on to teach experimental animation at CalArts Film & Video School and has been a professor at Tsinghua’s Arts and Design Academy since 2022. His short “Missing One Player” won a Prix Ars Electronica and a Silver Dove at DOK Leipzig in 2015.

	His mid-length documentary “Breathless Animals” debuted in the Berlinale Forum in 2019 and was named best mid-length documentary at Iran’s Cinéma Vérité. His first animated feature, “Silver Bird and Rainbow Fish,” premiered in the Tiger Competition at the International Film Festival Rotterdam in 2022.

	Founded in 2014, Asian Shadows sells Asian films by Asian directors worldwide. Its recent titles include Eddie Cahyono’s “Ibuku,” which won the Busan Award Special Jury Prize at this year’s Busan International Film Festival, and “The Seoul Guardians,” directed by Kim Jong-woo, Kim Shin-wan and Cho Chul-young, which picked up a Netpac Award special mention in Rotterdam. The company’s catalog also includes Wang Bing’s “Man in Black,” Soda Kazuhiro’s “The Cats of Gokogu Shrine” and Mouly Surya’s “This City Is a Battlefield.”

	“Vertigo Garden” is the third Lei film handled internationally by the company, after “Breathless Animals” and “Silver Bird and Rainbow Fish.”

title: ‘Hamnet’ Play From Royal Shakespeare Company Sets First U.K. Tour
description: The Royal Shakespeare Company‘s stage version of “Hamnet,” Lolita Chakrabarti’s adaptation of Maggie O’Farrell’s novel about William Shakespeare’s
body:
The Royal Shakespeare Company‘s stage version of “Hamnet,” Lolita Chakrabarti’s adaptation of Maggie O’Farrell’s novel about William Shakespeare’s family and the death of his 11-year-old son, will tour the U.K. for the first time starting in September 2027.

	Fiery Angel and Neal Street Productions are presenting the RSC production, which previously played London’s West End. The tour will open Sept. 25, 2027, at Lowry in Salford, England. It will then move on to Newcastle, Truro, Norwich, Nottingham, Canterbury, Birmingham, Glasgow and Bath before pausing for Christmas.
	

	According to the producers, performances will pick up again in 2028 with dates in Belfast, York, Wimbledon and Southampton. More dates will be added later. Casting and the rest of the creative team have yet to be announced.

	Erica Whyman, the RSC’s former deputy and acting artistic director, directs, with sets by Tom Piper. The play opened at the company’s Swan Theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon in 2023 and set box office records there. Later that year it moved to the Garrick Theatre in the West End, opening with the biggest advance the venue had seen up to that point. Whyman has also taken the production on a U.S. tour.

	The story begins in Warwickshire in 1582, when Agnes Hathaway, a healer, meets William Shakespeare, who is working as a Latin tutor. The two build a life and a family together. After the plague kills their son Hamnet, each parent is left to grieve alone.

	O’Farrell’s novel won the Women’s Prize and the National Book Critics Circle Award. It has since become an Oscar-winning film, which Neal Street also produced.
	

	“It’s wonderful to know that the RSC/Neal Street production of ‘Hamnet’ is embarking on a tour of the U.K.,” O’Farrell said. “The production goes from strength to strength and it’s lovely that more people will get to see it.”

	Chakrabarti’s earlier stage adaptation of Yann Martel’s “Life of Pi” won the Olivier Award for best new play. It reached Broadway in March 2023 and picked up five Tony nominations there. Her debut play, “Red Velvet,” began at London’s Tricycle Theatre before runs in New York and the West End.

	Chakrabarti said she had felt keenly the weight of making the historical figures relatable and bringing them back to life. “William Shakespeare’s reach is beyond compare and everyone without exception has some knowledge of his life, his works, his stories and his language,” she said. “To try and humanize a man of such reach is a humbling thing. But in the end, this is a story about family – an eleven year old boy and the people around him.”

	Whyman has previously run Southwark Playhouse, the Gate Theatre in London and Northern Stage in Newcastle. She called Chakrabarti’s script deft, funny and highly accessible. “It is a love story with a remarkable woman and her family at its heart, but it is also a love letter to the theater, to Shakespeare and the miraculous capacity of the human imagination,” she said. “I have spent my career advocating for U.K. touring so I’m especially pleased to be working with Fiery Angel and Neal Street so that we can share this production with so many new audiences all over the country.”

	The tour schedule is as follows:

	The Lowry, Salford: Sept. 25–Oct. 2, 2027Theatre Royal Newcastle: Oct. 5–9, 2027Hall for Cornwall, Truro: Oct. 12–16, 2027Norwich Theatre Royal: Oct. 19–23, 2027Theatre Royal Nottingham: Oct. 26–30, 2027Marlowe Theatre, Canterbury: Nov. 2–6, 2027The Alexandra, Birmingham: Nov. 9–13, 2027Theatre Royal Glasgow: Nov. 16–20, 2027Theatre Royal Bath: Nov. 23–27, 2027Grand Opera House, Belfast: Jan. 18–22, 2028Grand Opera House, York: Feb. 1–5, 2028New Wimbledon Theatre, London: March 7–11, 2028Mayflower Theatre, Southampton: March 21–25, 2028

	Neal Street is a Banijay Entertainment company founded in 2003 by Sam Mendes, Pippa Harris and Caro Newling. On stage it also originated “The Lehman Trilogy” and “The Hills of California.” On the film side, it is in production on Mendes’ Beatles project for Sony Pictures, which is made up of four separate theatrical features.

schema.headline: ‘Hamnet’ Play From Royal Shakespeare Company Sets First U.K. Tour

title: Oliver Laxe on Overcoming His Fears, Making Films as an Act of ‘Prayer’ and Allowing His ‘Wounds’ to Drive Him to ‘Take the Leap’
description: Oscar-nominated Spanish director Oliver Laxe opened up about the fear, vulnerability and self-doubt that undergird his work as a filmmaker, confess
body:
Oscar-nominated Spanish director Oliver Laxe opened up about the fear, vulnerability and self-doubt that undergird his work as a filmmaker, confessing in a deeply personal appearance at the Thessaloniki Film Festival that his career was born in part out of a “need to protect” himself.

	“Many times I am afraid to express what I truly have inside of me. Sometimes, I end up thinking: ‘You make a film that maybe no one will watch, but you can count on becoming a better person through this process.’ And I take the leap,” he said.
	

	“I am a particularly fragile person, and my decision to become a director is to a great extent related with my need to protect myself. The crises we have suffered enable us to comprehend more deeply our inner world. ‘Sirat’ aspired to bring people faced up against death.”

	Laxe was invited to this year’s Thessaloniki festival to curate a special programming sidebar, “Welcome to the Desert,” selecting 17 films — from the 1930s until the present day — set in the desert, including David Lean’s seven-time Oscar winner “Lawrence of Arabia,” Dennis Hopper’s seminal 1969 road movie “Easy Rider” and a pair of the director’s own films: the 2016 Cannes Critics’ Week prizewinner “Mimosas” and his 2025 dual-Oscar-nominated “Sirat.”

	Laxe, who won the Thessaloniki Film Festival’s Golden Alexander in 2019 with his Un Certain Regard prize-winning “Fire Will Come,” appeared in conversation with programming head Yorgos Krassakopoulos to talk about his artistic process and the spiritual element running through the tribute program.
	

	“The desert is like a mirror. There, you cannot escape yourself, you cannot hide. You are called to confront what you are really made of,” he said. “In our everyday lives, we find ourselves in a state of constant distraction. In the desert you need to be alert, to be present, and that is one of its most enchanting elements in my view.”

	Reflecting on how the theme of this year’s tribute resonated within his own films, he went on to describe such desert encounters as a kind of journey, drawing on his own deeper need for connection. “I am searching for love. I, too, seek a way to cross the desert. I have wounds,” he said.

	The director’s fourth feature, “Sirat,” which competed for the Palme d’Or at last year’s Cannes Film Festival, was partly filmed on location in Morocco’s Saraha Desert. Praised by Variety’s Jessica Kiang as “a brilliantly bizarre, cult-ready vision of human psychology tested to its limits,” it follows a father and his son searching for his daughter, who vanished after attending a rave in the desert.

	That dusty, scorched landscape serves as more than just a backdrop for the film, taking center stage in Laxe’s probing investigation into the human psyche. Speaking in Thessaloniki, the director explained that the belief that nature “possesses a transcendental quality” is essential to his cinematic worldview.

	“When surrounded by nature, you sense how meaningless you are in contrast with its infinitude. As a film director, I too succumb to arrogance,” he said. “We believe we have the power to change the world, and every once in a while we could use a reminder that we are not in control of everything.

	“Very often, while shooting, we get frustrated because things do not go as expected,” he continued. “Months later, we rewatch the material and we come to understand that it is beautiful exactly because it is gifted with a touch of the unexpected. Life has its own way to create images, and sometimes you just need to accept it.”

	A French-born filmmaker, who moved to his parents’ native Galicia as a young boy, Laxe spent a formative period of his life in Morocco, where he also filmed “Mimosas” and the 2010 docufiction “You All Are Captains.” It was an experience that shaped his views on both filmmaking and the world, with Laxe explaining how his encounters with Islamic culture highlighted the need for empathy, and a reexamination of how we observe and represent “the Other” in film.
	

	“We, as Western people, suffer from a great deal of guilt, often choosing to handle it by pointing the finger and blaming ‘the Others,’” he said. “We are still amidst a de-colonization process. The best way to observe other people is by placing yourself in their position. You have to be willing to meet them, to forge a bond and accept how this encounter can transform you.”

	Such transformation, he later added, pointed to the deeply spiritual nature of so much of his work.

	“To me, film directing is like a prayer,” he said. “It is my way to celebrate life’s complexity, express my gratitude for being alive and feel connected with anything occurring around me.”

	The Thessaloniki Film Festival runs Nov. 5 – 15.

schema.headline: Oliver Laxe on Overcoming His Fears, Making Films as an Act of ‘Prayer’ and Allowing His ‘Wounds’ to Drive Him to ‘Take the Leap’

title: ‘The Bureau’ Producer Federation Studios Moves to Recapitalize as Lionel Uzan Succeeds Pascal Breton as President
description: Federation Studios, the Paris-based group behind French spy series “The Bureau,” is overhauling its finances and leadership, with co-founder Lionel
body:
Federation Studios, the Paris-based group behind French spy series “The Bureau,” is overhauling its finances and leadership, with co-founder Lionel Uzan succeeding Pascal Breton as president and Montefiore and the company’s financial shareholders set to take majority control.

	The company said Thursday that it settled on the plan after weighing a number of strategic alternatives. An upcoming capital increase will shore up its equity and cut its debt substantially, giving it the resources to grow faster. Every one of its longtime financial and banking partners is backing the move.
	

	When the deal closes, majority ownership will pass to Montefiore and the group’s financial backers.

	Federation Studios is also narrowing its focus. It will concentrate on the markets it sees as having the most potential, and on scripted programming, where it counts itself among Europe’s top players.

	The leadership change follows 12 years of partnership between the two founders. Uzan will be supported by an executive board made up of Éric Broet, Cosette Liebgott, Simona Rapino and Chiraz Zribi.

	Breton has been named chair of the supervisory board. He stays closely involved in the company’s growth, both as a shareholder and as a producer.

	Federation Studios brings together more than 30 production companies across seven countries. Among them are Federation Studio France – which the group says has been France’s top drama producer for several years running – along with Bonne Pioche, Cheyenne Federation, Federation Stories, Fabula Pictures, Empreinte Digitale, Habanita Federation, Picture Perfect Federation and Federation Spain.
	

	Distribution arm Federation International handles both in-house and third-party titles. Its catalog spans all five seasons of “The Bureau,” plus “In Treatment,” “Around the World in 80 Days,” “Find Me in Paris,” “Bardot,” the eight-season “Deadly Tropics” and “Sherlock & Daughter.” Recent additions include “A Tale of Two Cities,” “I, Jack Wright,” now in its second season, “Dustfall” and “Lucky Luke.”

title: Bollywood Romance ‘Weekend’ Eyes First Indian Feature Shoot in Russia’s Yakutia as Picture Perfect Signs MoU With Sakhafilm, Saidam Baryl (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Indian romantic drama “Weekend” is eyeing a shoot in Russia’s remote Sakha Republic, also known as Yakutia, after producer Vivek Singhania’s banner
body:
Indian romantic drama “Weekend” is eyeing a shoot in Russia’s remote Sakha Republic, also known as Yakutia, after producer Vivek Singhania’s banner Picture Perfect signed a memorandum of understanding with local outfits Saidam Baryl and Sakhafilm to explore taking the production there.

	The three-way MoU was signed during the recently concluded 9th Yakutsk International Film Festival. If the film goes ahead, it would be the first Indian feature shot in the region, which lies in Russia’s Far East and has built a reputation for some of the country’s most singular indie filmmaking.
	

	The story follows Varun and Kaya, two young people whose chance meeting turns into a weekend that alters their lives. The project was first developed around Indian locations, and the producers are now weighing a reworked version that draws on Yakutia’s scenery and culture. Possible locations include the regional capital Yakutsk, the Lena River, the Lena Pillars – a UNESCO World Heritage Site – and isolated rural villages. The region’s summer white nights could also give the romance an unusual look.

	“Indian cinema has always had the power to take audiences to extraordinary destinations,” said Singhania, producer and founder of Picture Perfect. “Yakutia offers landscapes, culture and visual possibilities that Indian audiences have rarely experienced on screen. We are excited to explore how ‘Weekend’ could bring these two worlds together through a story with universal emotional appeal. I believe this collaboration could open a new and exciting chapter between Indian cinema and the filmmakers of Yakutia.”
	

	Under the proposed setup, Saidam Baryl and Sakhafilm would be the film’s principal local production partners. Picture Perfect will explore development and look for Indian production partners. Saidam Baryl will weigh local production, creative adaptation and coordination on the ground, while Sakhafilm will look at contributing infrastructure, technical resources, local know-how and access to filming locations.

	Stepan Burnashev, the filmmaker and producer who heads Saidam Baryl and serves as executive director of the Sakha Filmmakers Association, said international co-production means more than just bringing foreign crews to Yakutia. “It is about creating meaningful creative partnerships, exchanging experience and telling stories that can connect with audiences across cultures. India has one of the world’s largest and most influential film industries, and we see great potential in working together. ‘Weekend’ could become an important first step toward a long-term relationship between our film communities.”

	Singhania and Burnashev started talking earlier this year, and Picture Perfect sent a formal letter of interest in June. The new pact brings Sakhafilm, the republic’s state film company, to the table as a prospective local production partner.

	Alexey Egorov, general director of Sakhafilm, said the region now has a homegrown industry built on skilled filmmakers, seasoned crews and one-of-a-kind locations, and that the company sees working with international partners as a way to keep it growing. “The possibility of bringing an Indian feature film to Yakutia is particularly exciting, as it could open new opportunities for our local professionals and introduce our region to millions of Indian moviegoers,” Egorov said. “We hope this partnership will become a starting point for future collaborations between the film industries of India and Yakutia.”

	The partners are also eyeing a tourism bump. Singhania’s earlier films and web series featured locations including Germany, London, Paris, Dublin, Bangkok and Muscat. According to the producer, those titles sparked travel interest among Indian viewers at home and in the diaspora, with tourism boards logging more inquiries from fans keen to visit the locations.

	Next comes reworking the script for a Yakutia setting, working out production needs and lining up financing and Indian production partners. A location scout is being considered for 2027. The MoU is non-binding, and the money, the shooting schedule and how the co-production will be structured have yet to be settled.
	

	Singhania’s credits include Bollywood features “Na Tum Jaano Na Hum” and “Chura Liyaa Hai Tumne,” along with consulting producer roles on “Namastey London,” “Aap Kaa Surroor,” “Badass Ravikumar” and “Dishkiyaaoon.” His international work includes “Hexing,” “Karma: Crime Passion Reincarnation,” “Seal Team Six: The Raid on Osama Bin Laden” and “Indisch fur Anfanger.”

	Saidam Baryl, which focuses on independent films and international collaboration, is behind titles including “Black Snow,” “Yt,” “Aita” and “The Penthouse.” Sakhafilm has been involved in internationally acclaimed titles “The Lord Eagle” (2018), “The Sun Above Me Never Sets” (2019) and “Don’t Bury Me Without Ivan” (2022).

	The deal is part of a wider push by the Yakutsk festival to connect local filmmakers with overseas producers, especially from Asia, and to sell the region to foreign productions as a creative collaborator as well as a place to shoot.

schema.headline: Bollywood Romance ‘Weekend’ Eyes First Indian Feature Shoot in Russia’s Yakutia as Picture Perfect Signs MoU With Sakhafilm, Saidam Baryl (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Ghost Soldier’ Review: Jim Caviezel Is a Superheroic Soldier in an Uninspired, Retrograde Actioner
description: If “Walk Hard” was the parody that made it harder to take seriously subsequent music biopics, “MacGruber” did the same for a certain subset of acti
body:
If “Walk Hard” was the parody that made it harder to take seriously subsequent music biopics, “MacGruber” did the same for a certain subset of action movies. Directed by William Eubank (“Underwater”), “Ghost Soldier” stacks up one-man-army cliches as early as the opening credits and continues as if no one’s ever told the story of an individual with a certain set of skills defending the sovereignty of blue-collar Americans from deep-pocketed and unscrupulous foreign interests.
	

	Jim Caviezel, who’s increasingly made himself a Hollywood representative for politically conservative ideologies with projects like “Infidel” and “Sound of Freedom” (not to mention a series of faith-based projects that began with “The Passion of the Christ”), does little to dispel that association as this film’s tireless, technologically advanced and morally upright title character. But Eubank’s glossy direction, paired with a merciless urgency (and complete lack of originality) in Chris Papsadero’s script, renders the story’s ripped-from-the-headlines details with too little dimensionality even for it to deliver the satisfaction of a good, bloody B-movie.

	Caviezel plays Henry “Fitz” Fitzgerald, a former Special Forces soldier who retires to Valentine, Wyoming to live in relative anonymity while still designing advanced weapons for DARPA, the Department of Defense’s research and development agency. When “water monetization” company Brownstone begins buying up land around Midwest rivers and lakes for sale to AI companies for their data centers, its CEO (Mido Hamada) instructs his U.S. representative Ty Bell (Alexej Manvelov) to apply pressure — financial or physical — to coerce holdouts in Valentine.
	

	Using enforcers Graves (Garret Dillahunt) and McNeil (Ricky Whittle), Bell tries to bully the nearby Hernandez family into yielding their property, first by declaring eminent domain and later by setting their home on fire. After befriending the Hernandez’ young son Jack (Cameron Gayden), Fitz steps in to protect them using a variety of cutting-edge weapons he has stored in a bunker below his own home. After Graves realizes that the former soldier will present a bigger problem even than his armed “security team” can handle, Brownstone sends in a well-trained group of mercenaries led by Mirko (Beau Knapp) to flush him out and deliver the remaining parcels of land. Aided by gun dealer Garry (Michael Ironside) and a sheriff, Heidi (Olivia Thirlby), who ran afoul of corrupt local leadership, Fitz announces plans to exact vengeance against bloodthirsty Mirko and drive Brownstone out of Valentine permanently.

	Released Stateside on Veterans Day, “Ghost Soldier” clearly aims to pay tribute to America’s servicemen and women, and Papasadero’s script firmly sides with hard working citizens who too often in real life get crushed by the money and muscle of corporate interests. But even if the family Fitz is protecting from Blackstone is a Latino one whose patriarch died in combat, the film unnecessarily tries to generate patriotic sentiment by making the company’s CEO a ruthless Bahranian who doesn’t hesitate to bring in bloodthirsty soldiers to commit an extrajudicial killing or 10 in order to achieve his avaricious goals. 

	Such xenophobic dog whistles might be common (or even expected) in productions from The Daily Wire, but it’s more surprising in a wide release from Sony Pictures. But then again, nothing else in the film has been thought through in any depth, so such details feel more like the most direct means to an end — in other words, instantly establishing good versus evil — than an attempt to make an actual political statement.

	Instead, the movie opens with dialogue in which Fitz in spoken of in comically hushed tones (“there’s only one guy for this task”) and then abdicates all other character development in service of making him seem like the ultimate badass. Strictly speaking, there’s nothing wrong with that, but most of what makes Fitz such an effective soldier is his arsenal of futuristic gear, from night vision goggles to clothing that camouflages him in plain sight to bullets that bend around objects, splinter into explosive fragments or use homing devices to hit their targets. That bag of tricks makes him more like Iron Man than a righteous, proletariat-defending warrior, and it undermines what, again, seems designed at least in part to be a rousing paean to those who serve.
	

	The further problem is Caviezel, who successfully sells his role as a super-soldier but fails to inject any deeper humanity in Fitz  beyond the fact that he befriends a young boy. In retrospect, it feels like Terrence Malick figured out his appeal back in “The Thin Red Line,” at least as far as military roles are concerned: He’s a cipher, a silhouette for the audience to project their feelings upon. That certainly helps amplify Fitz’s drive, focus and intensity, but what he achieves in the film’s inevitable conclusion feels less like justice than retribution — which rings hollow.

	Remarkably, Eubank assembles a fairly impressive ensemble of character actors, including Dillahunt, Knapp, Ironside and Thirlby, as well as Shea Whigham as Fitz’s government liaison and Jaina Lee Ortiz as Jack’s widowed mom Sophia. Unfortunately, as either his friend or foe, they have little to do except fear or admire him. At 90 minutes, “Ghost Soldier” doesn’t have the patience or interest to populate Fitz’s world with anything but victims, worshippers or targets, which is unfortunate because it ends with the implication that the film’s distributor would love to expand his saga into a larger universe where he’s dropped into international conflicts to single-handedly resolve them.

	There are, of course, dozens of stories — single-serving or franchise-built — about soldiers brandishing their skill set off the battlefield, so one more doesn’t materially impact that well-established canon. But the ones that endure are the ones that elicit an audience response, be it excitement, empathy or even tragedy. By comparison, “Ghost Soldier” has the spontaneity of a training exercise that’s been run too many times.

schema.headline: ‘Ghost Soldier’ Review: Jim Caviezel Is a Superheroic Soldier in an Uninspired, Retrograde Actioner

title: Tom Holland Says Starring in ‘The Odyssey’ Has Given Him an ‘Ambition to See What Else is Out There For Me’
description: Tom Holland has starred in two of this year’s biggest-grossing films – “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “The Odyssey” – but he says it’s the latter
body:
Tom Holland has starred in two of this year’s biggest-grossing films – “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “The Odyssey” – but he says it’s the latter that will impact the next stage of his career.

	At a screening of Christopher Nolan’s Greek epic in London on Thursday, Holland was asked what he’d taken away from the experience, in which he plays Odysseus’ son Telemachus, to which he replied: “I’d probably say it’s confidence and an ambition to see what else is out there for me.”
	

	“I’ve been an admirer of Chris since I can remember, and to have the opportunity to work with him and to have his approval, and to sit in his house and watch his movie and to get a pat on the back, for me, just was like the perfect way for me to start whatever it is that I’m doing next,” Holland explained. “He’s given me a level of confidence as an actor that I don’t know if I had before and I’m very grateful that that is something that I can take away from this.”

	Holland said that while he has also learned a lot from his fellow actors (which included his wife Zendaya) and crew members, he would be going into his next project “with this sense of achievement and this newfound confidence in what I think I can do” thanks to Nolan’s film. “That is what Chris and Emma do so well, is they really champion their actors,” he said.

	The actor, who has played Spider-Man for over a decade, is understood to be in pre-production for a Fred Astaire biopic which will see him return to his dancing roots, given that Holland’s entry into showbiz was via the West End stage production of “Billy Elliot.”
	

	Robert Pattinson, who plays the scheming Antinous in “The Odyssey,” joined Holland at the screening in London, where he also reflected on working with Nolan and his wife and producing partner Emma Nolan, saying the couple make filmmaking look “effortless.”

	Underscoring the point, Pattinson, who is currently in London filming “The Batman: Part II,” revealed he lives next door to the couple in the Los Angeles neighborhood of Los Feliz, where he saw the Nolans holding a bake sale on their drive just days before they flew out to start shooting “The Odyssey,” undoubtedly the most ambitious project of their careers.

	“It’s like a week out from shooting, and [Emma] had made about a million cakes, which were delicious, like incredible cakes, and she stayed all day,” Pattinson marvelled. “It was for a charity, and she’s like selling cakes in the driveway, to the neighbors, all day. This is about five days before the shoot. Her and Chris. I was literally like, this is the craziest thing I’ve ever seen.”

	“I was literally just walking past. I’m like, ‘Oh, you’re still doing the cakes?’” he laughed. “It’s wild. They’re  just on another level of calm.”

	As well as shooting for three months across six countries on both land and sea, “The Odyssey” is the first feature film to be shot entirely on Imax 70mm film cameras (Nolan shot more than 2 million feet of film.)

	“I think what’s so amazing about Chris is that he’s able to create scale, but without sacrificing the heart and soul of what makes the characters tick,” Holland said during the sceening, which was held at the 65-feet high BFI Imax theater in London.

	“The beauty of the Imax camera is that it almost like looks into your soul,” he continued. “You know, like you have stage acting, and then it kind of goes to film acting, and there’s a difference. And then I think there’s even a bigger difference to IMAX acting.”

	But there was one – large drawback – he said. Glancing at the enormous screen behind him, Holland quipped “I was very upset about my pimple opening the movie. It literally is the opening scene. First time you see me, it’s like right there.”

schema.headline: Tom Holland Says Starring in ‘The Odyssey’ Has Given Him an ‘Ambition to See What Else is Out There For Me’

title: Late Billionaire Ted Turner: Ex-Wife Jane Fonda Not Named in 2025 Will
description:
Late Billionaire Ted Turner
                          No Mention of Ex-Wife Jane Fonda in Will
body:
Late Billionaire Ted Turner
                          No Mention of Ex-Wife Jane Fonda in Will
                          Left His Children In Charge
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 12, 2026
                            12:00 AM PST
                                                                            
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Late businessman Ted Turner was married and divorced three times during his life ... but the final version of his will made no mention of his last and legendary ex-wife, Jane Fonda ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Ted’s children, Laura, Robert, Rhett, Reed and Sara, filed a petition to be named executors of the CNN founder’s estate. They were the only listed heirs to Ted’s fortune.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The filing notes that Ted was married three times during his life. His ex-wives included Judy Nye, who he divorced in 1964, Jane Turner, who he split with in 1988, and Jane Fonda, but the marriage ended in 2001.
      

            Jane is not listed as a beneficiary to the estate ... despite her raving about her ex-husband for years after the split ... and praising him after he passed.
      
    
            Ted reportedly made several changes to his trust, which was first drafted in 2003, when he was 64. He changed the trust again in 2005 … made more changes in 2006 and 2007 … and again in 2009, 2011, 2013, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and his final amendment in 2025.
      
    
            Ted instructed his heirs to pay his debts and handle business matters ... but noted, “I have confidence in the investments which will be found in my estate at the time of my death,” but said they could sell off assets, if needed.
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported, Ted died on May 6, 2026, at the age of 87.

            Looks like Jensen Huang's about to be out as Nvidia CEO ... amid reports of a rumored second affair with an exec who reported to him.
      
    
            People familiar with the matter told The Wall Street Journal the board is planning to meet ASAP to discuss ousting him after word got out about his multiple affairs.
      
    
            CNN reports that the board is meeting Wednesday night to decide Jensen's fate.

            Not only is Jensen on the chopping block for the company he founded, but now there's also a class action lawsuit against Nvidia because of the whole thing.
      
    
            Rough week.
